qs.q: Which autoantibody is classically positive in Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC), a condition involving bile duct destruction and pruritus?
qs.e: Primary Biliary Cholangitis is characterized by bile duct destruction and is positive for anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA). Antinuclear and smooth muscle antibodies are typically seen in autoimmune hepatitis.

qs.q: Which of the following serum autoantibodies is found in over 95% of patients with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)?
qs.e: Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) is found in over 95% of patients with PBC. SMA is typically associated with autoimmune hepatitis.

ai.title: Primary Biliary Cholangitis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Autoimmune destruction of intra‑hepatic bile ducts causing cholestasis, pruritus and fatigue. Diagnosis hinges on antimitochondrial antibody and cholestatic biochemistry; management centres on ursodeoxycholic acid and monitoring for cirrhosis.

sections.p: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic, immune‑mediated disease that destroys small intra‑hepatic bile ducts, leading to cholestasis and eventual cirrhosis. The diagnosis is made when two of the following are present: (1) cholestatic liver enzymes (ALP >1.5× ULN or GGT >2× ULN), (2) antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) positivity, (3) compatible liver biopsy showing non‑suppurative destructive cholangitis.
b: Histology: lymphocytic infiltrate, bile duct loss

t.b: Do they show cholestasis? Elevated ALP and GGT indicate bile duct injury.
Positive result confirms autoimmune bile duct destruction; negative does not exclude if clinical picture strong.
Rule out extra‑hepatic obstruction; normal ducts support intra‑hepatic disease.
Shows portal tract inflammation and bile duct loss; used if diagnosis uncertain or to stage disease.

sections.p: The Mayo Risk Score predicts 5‑year transplant‑free survival and guides therapy escalation. It incorporates age, bilirubin, albumin, INR and ALP. Staging on biopsy uses the Scheuer system (I–IV).

t.b: Calculates transplant‑free survival; high scores prompt earlier referral for transplant.
Stage IV indicates cirrhosis; management shifts to portal hypertension surveillance.

sections.p: PBC is autoimmune; the exact trigger is unknown but genetic susceptibility (HLA‑DRB1*08) and environmental factors (viral infections, herbal toxins) are implicated. In low‑resource settings, co‑infection with hepatitis B/C or schistosomiasis can coexist and worsen liver injury.

t.b: Screen to exclude viral hepatitis; positive result changes management.
Positive indicates possible additive hepatic fibrosis; treat with praziquantel.

sections.p: Patients usually complain of fatigue, pruritus, and mild jaundice. Physical exam may reveal xanthomas, splenomegaly, or stigmata of chronic liver disease if advanced.

t.b: Assesses need for bile acid sequestrants or cholestyramine.

sections.p: Baseline work‑up includes LFTs, AMA, viral serology, ultrasound, and, if available, FibroScan or MRCP to exclude extra‑hepatic obstruction.

t.b: Non‑invasive assessment of fibrosis; >12 kPa indicates cirrhosis.
Detects extra‑hepatic biliary obstruction; normal ducts support PBC diagnosis.

sections.p: Complications include cirrhosis, portal hypertension, hepatocellular carcinoma, and cholangiocarcinoma. Red flags are worsening jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy, or sudden weight loss.

t.b: Suggests advanced cholestasis or biliary obstruction.

sections.p: First‑line therapy is ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) to improve bile flow and delay progression. If inadequate response, consider obeticholic acid or fibrates. Supportive care includes bile acid sequestrants for pruritus, vitamin D and K supplementation, and lifestyle advice.

t.b: Improves cholestasis and prolongs survival; avoid if patient has severe liver failure.
Reduce pruritus by binding bile acids in gut.

sections.p: Patients should have LFTs and AMA every 6–12 months, ultrasound for cirrhosis surveillance, and vaccinations for hepatitis A/B. Counsel on avoiding hepatotoxic drugs and alcohol.

t.b: Protect against hepatitis A/B to prevent superimposed liver injury.

faq.q: Why is pruritus so severe in PBC?
faq.a: Bile acids accumulate in skin; they stimulate itch receptors.

exam: A 45‑year‑old woman with fatigue and pruritus has ALP 400 IU/L, GGT 350 IU/L, and positive AMA. What is the next best step? — Order a liver biopsy to confirm diagnosis if non‑invasive tests are inconclusive.
A patient with known PBC develops sudden jaundice and ascites. What is the most likely complication? — Acute decompensation of cirrhosis; assess for variceal bleeding and hepatic encephalopathy.
Why is ursodeoxycholic acid the first‑line treatment in PBC? — It improves bile flow, reduces cholestasis, and delays progression to cirrhosis.
A patient with PBC has a normal ultrasound. What does this suggest? — Intra‑hepatic cholestasis; extra‑hepatic obstruction is unlikely.
Which laboratory value best predicts long‑term survival in PBC? — Mayo Risk Score components, especially bilirubin and albumin.
A patient with PBC is on UDCA but still has pruritus. What is an appropriate adjunct therapy? — Bile acid sequestrants such as cholestyramine.
Why should patients with PBC avoid certain herbal remedies? — Many contain hepatotoxic compounds that can worsen liver injury.
